title: Foundational Gaps in the Smallpox Narrative: From Variolation to Eradication
content: The conventional account of Jenner’s cowpox vaccine attributes a series of enabling properties to pre-laboratory inoculation: harvesting, preserving and transmitting infectious material; attenuating disease first through variolation and again through cowpox substitution; and a visible ‘take’ validating the procedure. Applying Occam’s razor, this review considers simpler alternative explanations. A recurring pattern is revealed in which early assumptions became established premises that were insufficiently challenged even as scientific standards advanced. Thus, the take alone did not establish poxvirus transmission, and variolation’s 0.5–2% versus 20–30% mortality comparison improperly contrasted healthy recipients with patients already ill with smallpox. Jennerian vaccination inherited and compounded these limitations and was not demonstrably superior to contemporary refined variolation. The major/minor division did not independently explain the decline in smallpox burden, and the attributed 300-million twentieth-century death toll could not be substantiated from contemporary population-level mortality records. Most importantly, eradication coincided with a diagnostic discontinuity: 1978 marked both the first year without recognised naturally acquired cases and the first year in which laboratory confirmation became a de facto requirement for validating suspected smallpox outbreaks. These findings challenge the traditional interpretation of smallpox and its eradication.
